record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization
record.original_question: How can multi-objective evolutionary algorithms scale to many-objective optimization, where Pareto-dominance-based selection loses pressure because nondominated solutions grow rapidly with the number of objectives, and where the number of solutions needed to sample the Pareto front also grows rapidly?

evidence.quote: MOEAs that adopt a selection mechanism based on Pareto optimality do not scale properly
the number of solutions required to sample the Pareto front, also grows exponentially.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-objective optimization problem of the form: minimize $F(x) = (f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_m(x))$ subject to $x \in \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where $m \geq 4$ (the "many-objective" regime). A point $x \in \Omega$ is said to Pareto-dominate $y \in \Omega$ if $f_i(x) \leq f_i(y)$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ with strict inequality for at least one $i$. The Pareto-optimal set is $\{x \in \Omega : \nexists\, y \in \Omega \text{ with } y \prec x\}$, and its image under $F$ is the Pareto front.

A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a population-based stochastic search procedure that, in each generation, applies variation operators and a selection operator to a finite multiset (population) $P \subset \Omega$, aiming to converge to a representative finite approximation of the Pareto front. Selection mechanisms based purely on Pareto-dominance suffer two scalability obstructions as $m$ grows:

(i) The expected fraction of mutually nondominated points in a random population tends to $1$, so dominance-based selection loses selective pressure.

(ii) The number of points required to maintain an $\varepsilon$-cover of an $(m-1)$-dimensional Pareto front grows as $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(m-1)})$, making representative finite populations infeasibly large.

Problem. Design and rigorously analyze a class of selection and archiving mechanisms for MOEAs (e.g., based on decomposition into scalarized subproblems, indicator-based selection such as the hypervolume indicator, reference-point or reference-direction methods, or relaxed dominance relations) such that, for problems with arbitrarily many objectives $m$:

(a) the algorithm maintains positive and quantifiable selective pressure toward the Pareto front as $m \to \infty$;

(b) the population size required to achieve a prescribed approximation quality (measured by a chosen quality indicator, e.g., hypervolume difference, generational distance, or $\varepsilon$-dominance) grows at most polynomially in $m$;

(c) provable convergence and run-time guarantees can be established on a benchmark family of test problems.

Provide such an algorithmic framework together with the corresponding theoretical guarantees, or prove an impossibility result establishing lower bounds that preclude (a)–(c) simultaneously.
artifact.status_search_result: Scalability of MOEAs to many objectives remains an active open research area. While partial advances exist (decomposition-based methods such as MOEA/D, indicator-based methods using hypervolume, and reference-point methods such as NSGA-III), no method provides simultaneous polynomial-population guarantees, convergence proofs, and maintained selective pressure for arbitrary $m$; surveys consistently list many-objective scalability as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: A Survey of Multiobjective Evolutionary Algorithms Based on Decomposition
status_evidence.snippet: Decomposition-based MOEAs (e.g., MOEA/D) have been proposed to address many-objective optimization, but scalability and theoretical guarantees remain partially understood.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress via decomposition; full scalability theory still lacking.

status_evidence.title: NSGA-III: An Evolutionary Many-Objective Optimization Algorithm Using Reference-Point-Based Nondominated Sorting Approach
status_evidence.snippet: Reference-point methods extend dominance-based selection to many objectives, with empirical but limited theoretical guarantees.
status_evidence.claim: Heuristic many-objective methods exist; rigorous guarantees on population size and convergence remain open.
